pr_title: Extended resolve default cache to improve the resiliency and protect from DNS infrastructure failure and outages
pr_body:
Introduces a new feature, the `StaleRetentionSec` flag, to the systemd-resolved service. This flag allows users to enhance DNS resiliency by utilizing the serve stale feature, which safeguards client applications from DNS server failures. This feature is an implementation inspired by the DNS Serving Stale Data mechanism outlined in [RFC 8767](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8767/). 

When the `StaleRetentionSec `property is set, the systemd-resolved service retains DNS resource records in the cache longer than their standard Time to Live (TTL), causing these records to be classified as stale data.  systemd-resolved responds with the stale data in case of DNS server failures or timeouts (except NXDOMAIN) to protect client applications from DNS-related disruptions.

If this is intending to implement RFC 8767, I think it should follow that RFC more closely? I've only given it a quick scan, but I think this PR is missing some things, like continuing to not cache any RR with a TTL of 0. I think this PR should both explicitly clarify (in code comments) that the 'serve_stale' option is an implementation of RFC 8767, as well as make sure the implementation adheres to that RFC.

After reading rfc8767, I think these are the main points:

1) This RFC overrides RFC2181, and requires the TTL to be interpreted as unsigned int, instead of signed int. Meaning the current code would need to stop converting "negative" (i.e. MSB set) ttl values to 0. (IMHO this RFC's reasoning seems right for all cases on this point).
2) While our current code caps TTLs at 2 hours (which IMHO seems FAR to short), this RFC recommends 7 days. Personally, I think 7 days (max TTL) is much more sensible than 2 hours, but in any case, *IFF* systemd-resolved is serving "stale" DNS data, it makes absolutely no sense to cap TTL values at 2 hours but then continue to serve "stale" data (which isn't actually stale).
3) The RFC recommends the "stale timer" be user-configurable.
4) The RFC states that any "stale" data provided MUST include a TTL greater than 0, but it recommends all "stale" DNS data use a TTL of 30 seconds. Personally I think this is very appropriate; any "stale" DNS data should not be cached (by clients) for long - meaning, we should not be telling clients that stale DNS data has long TTL values.
5) Any upstream (authoritative) response of NoError or NXDOMAIN "must" clear/replace any existing cached data. I think this is our code's current behavior; just listing here to be sure it's confirmed.

Also, note that the RFC makes clear that after a DNS TTL has expired, the resolver MUST attempt to get fresh data from its upstream nameserver; it CANNOT continue to serve stale data without first attempting to actually resolve the name first. And this really is critical; if systemd-resolved caches DNS entries long beyond their actual TTL *without* attempting to refresh stale DNS data, it will absolutely break users.

Looking over the current changes, I think this will be simpler and easier to manage if a separate 'expired' cache is used, instead of overloading ->until and adding ->until_valid. However, @poettering may disagree.

I also think this needs to adhere to the rfc, specifically the points in my [earlier comment](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/27681#issuecomment-1562069484).

@ddstreet  

-  Modified the server's stale flag from a Boolean to a timer, allowing users to customize the duration for retaining stale data.
- The default caching behavior remains unchanged, where data is not cached if the time-to-live (TTL) is less than zero.
- Additionally, if a query is answered using stale data, the TTL will be set to the minimum value between the record's TTL and 30 seconds.
- The 'Serve Stale' feature is designed to protect client applications from server failures such as timeouts or ServFail responses. But if we let negative responses  clear the cache, the whole point of the 'Serve Stale' thing would be lost. That's why I added the condition that if the 'Serve Stale' flag is on, only NXDomain or positive responses can clear the cache.

issue_context.title: [RFE] serving expired DNS records with systemd-resolved
issue_context.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Occasionally the upstream DNS service goes down (not replying) or misbehave (empty reply). From a client perspective, this outage is invisible, until the systemd-resolved cached entry expires and resolved tries to resolve a name once more.

When the cached entry expires, the DNS name resolution is attempted and fail. While this happens, authentication functions (using ldap or OpenID, that are usually configured using DNS names) fail, and a DNS outage turns into a bigger outage where clients cannot authenticate anymore to their service.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I wish resolved be able to serve stale entries (expired records). When the TTL expires, the entry is kept in the cache for some extra time until it can be resolved again.

[RFC 8767](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8767):

> This document defines a method (serve-stale) for recursive resolvers to use stale DNS data to avoid outages when authoritative nameservers cannot be reached to refresh expired data. One of the motivations for serve-stale is to make the DNS more resilient to DoS attacks and thereby make them less attractive as an attack vector.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
An alternative is to set an extra proxy such as CoreDNS that supports [this feature](https://github.com/coredns/coredns/issues/3158)

Another alternative could be to have a /etc/hosts.fallback file and write a nsswitch to use it when the previous entries fail... If you have other ideas I am interested.

**The systemd version you checked that didn't have the feature you are asking for**
Any version (currently running systemd-resolved-250~rc1-3.fc36.x86_64)

This (clamping dns TTL values to 2 hours, but also keeping "stale" records after we think they "expire") still makes no sense to me. Not sure if @poettering agrees with me or not.

The only benefit I can see for clamping TTL is to reduce how long records stay in our cache. However, if we are keeping the record in our cache past the clamped TTL, there really wasn't any point in clamping it at all, in fact clamping the TTL actually makes everything worse.

so my thinking was that overly long dns cache times don't really make sense on a client. we'd rather ask too often then too seldom. we are not a load-bearing DNS server for a bunch of clients, we are basically just an improvemet over the cache-less in-glibc resolver. Hence in the interest in being able to somewhat gracefully handle DNS misconfiguration i figured it makes sense to revalidate all entries after 2h no matter what, even if they are supposedly still valid for a year.

dunno. i tink this should be discussed separately from this PR.

so i looked into this in more detail. I think the confusion comes from the fact how CACHE_TTL_MAX_USEC is applied. 

If the stale logic is enabled it means that if a request comes in later than 2h after caching we'll try to refresh every record. If it works, then great, we'll return the refreshed RRset. But if it doesn't, then we'll return the stale data, up to the configured stale rentation timeout. 

If the stale logic is disabled it means that if a request comes in later than 2h after caching we'll try to refresh it. If it works, great. If not, we'll return an error.

I think this is a reasonable approach I think. The question of course is what is more important to people: honour superlong ttls because it allows taping over connectivity problems (A), or limit superlong ttls because it allows taping over DNS configuration problems (B). I think when figuring out the answer to this one should take into consideration whether one is looking at a DNS resolver such as resolved that is on the end-user's system such as systemd-resolved or whether one is looking at a DNS resolver at an ISP or so. An ISP DNS resolver will have many upstreams a client DNS resolver pretty much only one it strictly relies on.

I am still strongly of the opinion that having a stale cache makes no sense at all if we're continuing to clamp TTLs at 2 hours. RFC 8767 specifically recommends clamping at 1 week.

I don't know if it makes sense to unilaterally change this to 1 week for all users, regardless of the setting of the stale cache, but I am pretty sure if we are serving stale cache data, this really should be increased to 1 week. Otherwise, this results in the downsides of both approaches - it adds unnecessary network traffic and upstream dns server load to re-query something already in our cache, but also doesn't save us the reduced cache size that this clamp provides (because we're still caching it, just marking the expiry time as shorter than it actually is).
